The overlap signals cited in nomination (shared ancestors, same page, token overlap on 'listens'/'to') are proximity/wording signals only, so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment. judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade R (rank 0), Emergent Reading, Sub-strand 'Phonological/Phonemic Awareness', but in different terms: the first is Term 2 ('Divides multisyllabic words into syllables: uses clapping or drum beats... 'Lu-ne-tta' has three claps, 'Rose' one clap'), the second is Term 3 ('Segments oral sentences into individual words using words of one syllable first (e.g. Sam - is - a - boy)'). This is earlier-term to later-term within one grade, so first_to_second is the only admissible developmental direction. The change is substantive rather than repeated wording: oral segmentation moves from syllable units inside a single word to word units inside a whole sentence, and the Term 3 statement explicitly scaffolds on one-syllable words, so pupils who can hear and count syllables (recognising that 'Rose' is one clap) are better placed to isolate single-syllable words as discrete units in a spoken sentence. LC tags corroborate the shared phonological-awareness/segmenting strand. Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence (24 omitted source-evidence items each), so judgment rests on the printed bullets and LC text supplied; this limits but does not contradict the reading above.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in the Listening and Speaking (Oral) Skill Area, Term 1, and express the same core oral capability: talking about pictures in posters, theme charts and books. The Grade R endpoint (rank 0, sub-strand 'Daily activities in all areas of Language and other subjects') states it with the added coverage qualifier 'related to a minimum of five themes per term'; the Grade 1 endpoint (rank 1, sub-strand 'Twice weekly focussed listening and speaking activities') states the identical skill without that qualifier. The Grade 1 statement therefore shows no explicitly increased demand over the Grade R statement, and the differing sub-strand heading records how oral work is timetabled (daily programme vs twice-weekly focussed sessions) rather than evidence of expanded capability; the nomination signals are lexical overlap and weak rank proximity, which are similarity, not developmental, evidence. In this deliberately repetitive CAPS framework that is insufficient for buildsTowards. It is nonetheless more than generic repetition: the same picture- and book-talk capability is deliberately carried across adjacent grades within one Skill Area, giving pair-specific instructional coherence and reinforcement without dependency, so symmetric relatesTo with null direction is recorded. Confidence is moderate because the Grade R endpoint's source and supporting LC evidence are truncated, 24 source-evidence items are omitted for each endpoint, and both endpoints and their ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade 1 (rank 1) Reading and Phonics under the 'Daily Phonemic Awareness/Phonic Activities' Phonics sub-strand, but their identity scopes place the first in Term 1 and the second in Term 2, so an earlier-to-later-term developmental direction within the grade is permissible. The Term 1 statement is an emergent capability ('Begins to build up short words using sounds learnt such as c-a-t - cat'), i.e. blending taught single letter-sounds into short CVC words. The Term 2 statement extends this same phoneme-level work substantively: blending (h-op into hop) is retained but is combined with segmenting whole words into phonemes (hop into h-o-p) and consonant/vowel substitution word play (h->m in hop/mop), which require flexible manipulation of the sounds a learner has already learned to combine. The LC evidence confirms the Term 2 node decomposes into three distinct components (blending, segmenting, substitution) against the single blending component of the Term 1 node. Early facility in building short words from learnt sounds therefore supports success in the broader Term 2 phonemic-manipulation repertoire; this is expanded capability rather than generic repeated wording. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all nodes carry upstream audit/merge context, so judgment rests on the supplied statement texts, identity scopes and LCs.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are the identical CAPS Skill bullet "Reads own and others' writing" placed under the Paired/Independent Reading sub-strand of the Reading and Phonics skill area, but at different canonical grade coordinates: the second endpoint is Grade 2 (rank 2, Term 3) and the first is Grade 3 (rank 3, Term 2). This is the CAPS pattern of deliberately repeating a statement at a higher grade, where the same peer- and self-text reading routine is applied to the longer, more complex and more independently produced writing of Grade 3 learners, with greater reading independence expected. Proficiency at reading one's own and peers' writing in Grade 2 therefore supports success with the same routine in Grade 3, so the permitted lower-to-higher direction (Grade 2 -> Grade 3, second_to_first) is used. Evidence limitation: wording is literally identical and both endpoints' source evidence and supporting LC metadata are truncated, so the expansion is inferred from the grade coordinate and shared sub-strand context rather than from differing statement text; confidence is moderated accordingly.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade R (rank 0) Skills about rhyme, but at different terms and skill areas: the first is Term 2 / Emergent Reading / Phonological-Phonemic Awareness ('Identifies rhyming words in well known rhymes and songs', e.g. Humpty Dumpty), the second is Term 3 / Emergent Writing / Works with words ('Groups pictures of rhyming words, e.g. bat, cat, hat'). Direction Term 2 to Term 3 is permitted within Grade R. This is not mere repeated wording: recognising rhyme aurally inside familiar supported rhymes and songs is a less demanding phonological task than categorising isolated picture-named words by rime without a supporting text, so proficiency in the first plausibly supports success in the second. Shared LC tag 'phonological awareness'/'rhyming' corroborates the same underlying skill strand rather than establishing the edge on its own. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and both carry upstream merge/audit context, so judgment rests on the bounded statement text, identity scopes and LCs supplied.

They share genuine conceptual coherence around copying letters (LC tags 'copying', 'letters', 'writing'; LCs 'Copies words and letters onto paper' and 'Begins to copy letters and numerals ... in own writing attempts'), so the handwriting copying practice and the emergent pretend-writing use of copied letters mutually reinforce each other. However, they are parallel same-grade, same-term bullets in the same table row with no evidence of sequencing or of one being a substantive extension of the other: the handwriting item is motor/reproduction practice while the emergent writing item adds the conceptual writing/drawing distinction and self-initiated writing attempts. Same-rank, same-term placement plus shared ancestry and page proximity alone do not establish developmental direction, so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each), which limits further discrimination.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade 3 Writing Skills under the same 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' sub-strand (same Grade rank 3), differing by Term: the second SFI sits in Term 1 ('Uses subject-verb agreement correctly, e.g., I want / She wants'), the first in Term 2 ('Uses correct grammar so that others can read and understand what has been written'). The Term 1 statement targets one specific, exemplified grammatical convention, while the Term 2 statement generalises to controlling grammar across written text for reader comprehensibility; LC tags share 'grammar' and 'writing', with the Term 1 LC additionally tagged 'subject-verb agreement' and the Term 2 LC tagged 'clarity'. Mastery of the concrete agreement rule plausibly supports the broader goal of writing grammatically so readers can understand, so the permitted earlier-Term-to-later-Term direction (second_to_first) is used; the reverse within-grade direction would be invalid. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all ancestors carry upstream merge/audit context, so the Term banners and sub-strand headings should be read with that caveat; this limits but does not contradict the within-grade term ordering.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade R (resolved coordinate rank 0): the first under Term 2 / Listening and Speaking (Oral) ('Sings songs, recites rhymes and performs actions with the whole class'), the second under Term 3 / Emergent Reading / Emergent reading skills ('Draws pictures of stories, songs or rhymes'). The connection is genuine and pair-specific: the same oral text types (songs, rhymes) that learners perform orally with the whole class are the material they represent visually in the drawing task, so the two statements reinforce each other across modalities within one grade. But the evidence does not show substantive extension of a single capability - the second statement's new demand is drawing and visual meaning-making in a different skill area, not more letters, longer texts, greater independence, or an expanded oral repertoire. Nomination signals are lexical and structural (shared tokens 'songs'/'rhymes' at jaccard ~0.12-0.15, weak same-rank local proximity, a Grade-level shared ancestor), which cannot by themselves license a developmental claim. Canonical relatesTo (symmetric, null direction) therefore fits, rather than buildsTowards. Evidence limits: both endpoints have 24 omitted source-evidence items and all nodes carry upstream audit/merge context, so confidence is held moderate.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade R (rank 0) Skills: the first is Term 4 / EMERGENT WRITING / 'Works with words' — 'Copies short sentences and words written by the teacher'; the second is Term 3 / EMERGENT READING / 'Emergent reading skills' — 'Uses pictures to understand simple phrases and sentences in a book'. They are complementary emergent-literacy skills that both treat the printed word and sentence as meaningful units (reciprocal reading/writing print awareness at sentence level), which gives substantive conceptual coherence beyond the generic token overlap ('and', 'the', 'sentences') and the shared Grade R ancestor. However, the capabilities differ in kind — picture-supported meaning-making from text versus teacher-modelled transcription/copying — so the evidence does not show that proficiency in the Term 3 reading skill materially supports success in the Term 4 copying skill (or vice versa); no expanded-capability progression is documented between them. Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment rather than any directional buildsTowards. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), which limits deeper verification but does not make the available statement text ambiguous.
